evidence.claim: Valley farms and bluestone country connect two historic railroad viaducts.
evidence.quote: Featuring historic villages, rich valley farmland, and bluestone quarries, the 37.3-mile Viaduct Valley Way Scenic Byway

evidence.claim: Viaduct Valley Way runs between Lanesboro and Dixon in Pennsylvania’s Endless Mountains, through valley farmland and bluestone quarry country.
evidence.quote: Featuring historic villages, rich valley farmland, and bluestone quarries, the 37.3-mile Viaduct Valley Way Scenic Byway follows State Routes 171, 92, and 11 between Lanesboro and Dixon in the Endless Mountains region.

evidence.claim: VisitPA presents the 37.3-mile scenic byway as a drive linking historic villages and two railroad viaducts, Starrucca and Tunkhannock.
evidence.quote: the aptly named byway includes two of Pennsylvania’s most historic railroad viaducts along the way

evidence.claim: On PA 92, woodland alternates with fields, and the road winds beside Tunkhannock Creek into Nicholson.
evidence.quote: PA 92 winds east through more woodland with some fields to the north of the creek, heading into the borough of Nicholson

evidence.claim: The byway designation came in stages, beginning with sections of PA 92 in 2005.
evidence.quote: VIADUCT VALLEY WAY Effective: 2005 District: 4-0 County: Susquehanna State Route: 92

evidence.claim: In 2007, the Dixon-to-Lanesboro designation brought PA 92, PA 171 and two other state routes into the named journey.
evidence.quote: VIADUCT VALLEY WAY Effective: 2007 District: 4-0 County: Wyoming and Susquehanna State Route: 92, 171, 1009 and 1015 Dixon, PA to Lanesboro, PA.

evidence.claim: Another PA 92 segment in Oakland Township followed in 2012.
evidence.quote: VIADUCT VALLEY WAY Effective: 2012 District: 4-0 County: Susquehanna State Route: 92 Oakland Township.

evidence.claim: The bridges tell an older transportation story: Starrucca crossed a valley that the railroad had considered filling with an embankment.
evidence.quote: It was built to solve an engineering problem posed by the wide valley of Starrucca Creek. The railroad considered building an embankment, but abandoned the idea as impractical.

evidence.claim: Tunkhannock belonged to a cutoff replacing a winding, hilly rail route.
evidence.quote: The DL&W built the viaduct as part of its 39.6-mile (63.7 km) Nicholson Cutoff, which replaced a winding and hilly section of the route

evidence.claim: Begin at Starrucca near Lanesboro.
evidence.quote: Starrucca Viaduct is a stone arch bridge that spans Starrucca Creek near Lanesboro, Pennsylvania

evidence.claim: Susquehanna Depot brings the journey to the Susquehanna River.
evidence.quote: located on the Susquehanna River

evidence.claim: Southward, PA 92 links Jackson, South Gibson and Lenox through woods and farmland.
evidence.quote: After this interchange, the road heads through more forests with some fields and homes, crossing into Gibson Township and passing through South Gibson.

evidence.claim: Nicholson brings the concrete viaduct overhead.
evidence.quote: The route passes under the Tunkhannock Viaduct

evidence.claim: Beyond it, the creek-side road passes Starkville and East Lemon before reaching Dixon and US 6.
evidence.quote: PA 92 splits from US 6 by turning north onto an unnamed two-lane undivided road, passing through Dixon.

evidence.claim: PA 92 links Jackson, South Gibson and Lenox
evidence.quote: The route turns north again as it comes to an intersection with PA 106 in Lenox.

evidence.claim: PA 92 links Jackson, South Gibson and Lenox
evidence.quote: reaching an intersection with the eastern terminus of PA 492 in Jackson.

evidence.claim: the creek-side road passes Starkville and East Lemon
evidence.quote: PA 92 turns northeast and passes through East Lemon, turning east into farmland. The road enters Nicholson Township and heads into forests turning north as it continues alongside the Tunkhannock Creek. The route heads through more wooded areas with some homes and curves east, passing through Starkville.

evidence.claim: Starrucca’s stone arches answer a problem of width: the railroad abandoned a proposed embankment across the valley as impractical.
evidence.quote: It was built to solve an engineering problem posed by the wide valley of Starrucca Creek. The railroad considered building an embankment, but abandoned the idea as impractical.

evidence.claim: The New York and Erie Railroad built the crossing in 1847–48, using locally quarried bluestone, brick interior walls and concrete pier bases.
evidence.quote: built in 1847–48 by the New York and Erie Railroad, of locally-quarried random ashlar bluestone, except for three brick interior longitudinal spandrel walls and the concrete bases of the piers.

evidence.claim: Eight hundred workers completed it in a year.
evidence.quote: It took 800 workers, each paid about $1 per day, equal to $37.21 today, to complete the bridge in a year.

evidence.claim: The original broad-gauge track gave way to two standard-gauge tracks in 1886, and concrete reinforced the deck in 1958.
evidence.quote: The original single broad gauge track was replaced by two standard gauge tracks in 1886. The roadbed deck under the tracks was reinforced with a layer of concrete in 1958.

evidence.claim: The viaduct remains in railroad use.
evidence.quote: Still in use, the viaduct

evidence.claim: Susquehanna Depot made locomotives as well as receiving trains.
evidence.quote: In the past, railroad locomotives and railroad cars were made here.

evidence.claim: The railroad established workshops here while building its line through the county in 1848.
evidence.quote: The New York and Erie Railroad (later reorganized as the Erie Railroad) built a rail line through the county in 1848, including the Starrucca Viaduct: a monumental stone structure spanning Starrucca Creek. Concurrently, the railroad established workshops in what would eventually be known as Susquehanna Depot.

evidence.claim: The workforce eventually exceeded 1,000, and the complex included a 33-stall roundhouse, foundry and rail yard.
evidence.quote: they employed 700 workers by 1865, and later over 1,000. The complex included a 33-stall roundhouse, a rail yard, a foundry

evidence.claim: By 1887, the shops produced five locomotives a month.
evidence.quote: By 1887, the shops were producing five locomotives per month.

evidence.claim: The locomotive shops moved to Hornell in 1928.
evidence.quote: In 1928, the railroad relocated its locomotive shops to Hornell, New York

evidence.claim: The roundhouse closed in 1952 as Erie changed from steam to diesel.
evidence.quote: In 1952, Erie closed the roundhouse as it converted its steam locomotive roster to diesel locomotives.

evidence.claim: Most shop buildings were demolished in 1980 and 1981.
evidence.quote: Most of the railroad shop buildings were demolished in 1980 and 1981.

evidence.claim: At Nicholson, PA 92 passes beneath the Tunkhannock Viaduct.
evidence.quote: The route passes under the Tunkhannock Viaduct

evidence.claim: Almost half the bridge’s bulk lies underground.
evidence.quote: Almost half of the bulk of the bridge is underground.

evidence.claim: Above the creek bed, it rises 240 feet; measured from bedrock, its height reaches 300 feet.
evidence.quote: towers 240 feet (73.15 m) above the creek bed; it stands 300 feet (91.44 m) above bedrock.

evidence.claim: The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad opened it in 1915.
evidence.quote: Opened in 1915 by the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad (DL&W)

evidence.claim: It formed part of the Nicholson Cutoff, which shortened the rail journey by 3.6 miles and saved an hour for freight trains.
evidence.quote: The DL&W built the viaduct as part of its 39.6-mile (63.7 km) Nicholson Cutoff, which replaced a winding and hilly section of the route between Scranton, Pennsylvania, and Binghamton, New York, reducing travel by 3.6 miles (5.8 km)—21 minutes of passenger train time or one hour of freight train time.

evidence.claim: The concrete bridge still carries regular through freight daily.
evidence.quote: the bridge is still used daily for regular through freight service.

evidence.claim: The road passes beneath the Tunkhannock Viaduct, carrying Norfolk Southern’s Sunbury Line over both the highway and the creek.
evidence.quote: The route passes under the Tunkhannock Viaduct, which carries Norfolk Southern's Sunbury Line over the route and the Tunkhannock Creek

evidence.claim: At completion in 1848, it was the world’s largest stone railway viaduct, spanning Starrucca Creek near Lanesboro.
evidence.quote: Completed in 1848 at a cost of $320,000 (equal to $11,907,692 today), it was at the time the world's largest stone railway viaduct

evidence.claim: The Susquehanna station, opened in 1865, included a large hotel called Starrucca House.
evidence.quote: The Susquehanna railroad station, which included a large hotel called the Starrucca House, opened in 1865.

evidence.claim: Construction began in May 1912 with excavation for all 11 piers, reaching bedrock as much as 138 feet below ground.
evidence.quote: Construction on the bridge began in May 1912 by excavating all 11 bridge piers to bedrock, which was up to 138 feet (42 m) below ground.

evidence.claim: Valley farms and bluestone country connect two historic railroad viaducts.
evidence.quote: the aptly named byway includes two of Pennsylvania’s most historic railroad viaducts

evidence.claim: Starrucca and Tunkhannock.
evidence.quote: Starrucca Viaduct, the oldest stone railroad bridge still in use in Pennsylvania, and the Tunkhannock Creek Viaduct

evidence.claim: the concrete viaduct overhead.
evidence.quote: is a concrete deck arch bridge

evidence.claim: The concrete bridge still carries regular through freight daily.
evidence.quote: is a concrete deck arch bridge

flags: VisitPA gives 37.3 miles and routes 171, 92 and 11; PennDOT lists 92, 171, 1009 and 1015 for Dixon–Lanesboro. Exact corridor reconciliation remains unresolved. Driving order follows the strip map from Lanesboro toward Dixon.
The cache documents designation stages but no road builder or campaign narrative. Railroad construction is kept distinct from highway history.

No unsupported current moment claims were identified. The supported Nicholson tiger anecdote was omitted as unrelated. Susquehanna station dates differ between cache 04 (opened 1865) and 12 (built 1863); the narrative uses the opening date, not a construction date.
